newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST -Prospects for Britain's jobless improve.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -Prospects for Britain's jobless improve.

text.p: Britain's jobless rate is expected to continue falling steadily as the economy gears up to meet a surge in consumer demand, a Reuters survey of independent forecasts showed.
By third quarter 1998, unemployment is expected to fall to six percent, compared with the 6.9 percent posted in November, the mean of 29 forecasts in the survey showed.

"Unemployment will fall because the economy will grow strongly. This growth will be driven by domestic consumer demand. We see gains mainly in the services and financial sectors," said Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount.
"It's fallen by one percent over the last year and we see another percentage drop by the end of this year".
Union Discount predicts the unemployment rate will fall to 5.8 percent by end-1997.

At 4.7 percent by third quarter 1998, Liverpool Research Group predicts unemployment to dip below the official definition of full employment -- five percent -- and a 17-year low of 5.3 percent which Britain experienced in August 1980.

The unemployment forecasts were collected as part of a wider quarterly survey of British economic indicators, exchange and interest rates. Forty-two banks and research houses contributed to the survey, carried out between January 6 and 8.
Personal income boosted by higher wages and cash windfalls for millions of customers of building society flotations are given as reasons for the boost to demand.
Rising house prices have contributed to the 'feel-good' factor and people are moving. Demand for consumer durables is already on the up, analysts say.
Stuart Wetherby, UK economist at Panmure Gordon, also expects full employment at five percent by third quarter 1998.
"Given the way the labour market is tightening at the moment with an underlying trend of a 30,000 drop per month next year, I expect unemployment to keep falling" he said.
"This may moderate the following year, but I see no reason why it should moderate considerably, because I don't think long-term productivity trends have improved in the U.K."

Electronics industries are also expected to show considerable employment growth over the next two years, analysts said, partly reflecting the human resources and the billions of pounds which will have to be set aside to adapt computer systems to allow for the millenium.
Currently most computer systems use only the last two digits of the year. But with the change from 1999 to the year 2000, systems will have to be adapted to recognise the first two digits as well.

"The development of new technology and new products within the manufacturing sector are other reasons for growth in employment in the electronics industries," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
